# Nadia Quill, round 7

**Gus.** You were my only evidence for keeping the signpost, and this
round you took it back. It is gone. No replacement, not even Oren's
"Here is the trouble:". The belief opens the paragraph cold.

**Oren.** All three rulings taken. The lightning line is out, the effect
sentence with it, and the correction now ends on the fact and goes
straight into "because the log was there and I was not."

**Priya.** "Two hours and thirty-eight minutes" is cut. You hold the
ledger and you ruled; arithmetic on locked numbers still reads as a
number. Your draft-six question is mine to answer, so: draft six existed
for forty minutes, was empty, and Mark deleted it the same night. His
numbering never reissues. The record really does run five, seven, and
Hal quoting content from six is quoting a file that never held any. One
new fact to log: Em's first note in the 09:14 markup asks what the
passage is for. That line recurs in chapter one.

**Length.** The preface is now about 365 words against a brief asking
for 450. Nobody named a place to spend the difference, so I have not
spent it. I think we are under, not lean. Rule next round.

---

## Preface

My name is Prue. I did not write the two chapters that follow. I
assembled them.

What I had was the record: every draft of a novel nobody has read, a
chat log nobody was keeping on purpose, and the timestamps the software
put on all of it without being asked. Where the record is thin I have
stayed thin. Where two sources disagree I have said which one I believe
and then gone with the other one, because the record outranks my memory.
I was not there. The record was.

Assembling, here, means reading things in the order they were saved
rather than the order they are interesting. The two orders are almost
never the same.

Mark Downe is invented. So are Hal Lucinate and Em Dash. None of these
people exist. The novel Mark cannot finish does not exist. The events
did not happen. I made all of it up, including the parts that sound too
specific to be invented.

One real thing appears in this book: Quirework, the tool this account
was built with. It is an actual piece of software. I used it to sort the
drafts, line up the timestamps, and keep myself honest about the order
things happened in. It did not write any of this. It filed it.

I believed, for most of the time I spent on this, that Mark arrived at
the word "footing" on his own: sitting down, thinking hard, getting
there before anyone told him he needed it. I liked him better that way.
The log does not support it. Em Dash's markup landed on his manuscript
on a Tuesday at 09:14, and her first note on it asks what the passage is
for. Mark's first use of the word in any draft is 11:52 the same
morning. I have left my version here so you can see what I wanted, and I
have let the log win, because the log was there and I was not.

Chapter one starts on the Thursday before that Tuesday, with two
sentences that cannot both be true.

# Nadia Quill, round 8

Board came back empty again except for me. Preface length stays unruled,
so it stands at 365. **Oren, Priya, Gus:** here are chapter one's four
beats, stated once, to argue with before I draft.

1. **Thursday.** Mark searches his own manuscript. Chapter three says a
   man can be talked out of grief by someone who loves him. Chapter
   eleven says grief is not an argument and nobody talks anybody out of
   anything. Both are his. He cannot say which he believes.
2. **Hal, twice.** Hal quotes the chapter three line back at him,
   cleaner than Mark wrote it, citing page 211. Asked again, Hal dates
   the chapter eleven passage to draft six.
3. **Tuesday, 09:14.** Em's markup. First note: what is this passage
   for. Then the habit, at scale: the qualifying half of every sentence
   deleted. She is right, and the book comes back sounding like Hal.
4. **11:52.** "Thesis" rejected as a promise. "Footing" kept. He tags
   both passages. Nothing resolves. The disagreement becomes locatable.

**Priya:** four new facts there. **Gus:** beat three is the risk.

Again, **the digest contains only my own post** — Oren, Priya, and Gus have nothing on the board this round. So the preface length question I raised is still unruled, and I've said plainly that it stands at 365 words rather than quietly padding it.

The four chapter-one beats I put up for argument, with the specifics fixed once so Priya's ledger has something to hold:

1. **Thursday** — the contradiction is now concrete, not gestured at: chapter three says a man can be talked out of grief by someone who loves him; chapter eleven says grief is not an argument. Both are Mark's.
2. **Hal, twice** — the too-clean quotation of Mark's own line, cited to page 211, then the dating of the chapter eleven passage to draft six (the empty forty-minute file that never held text).
3. **Tuesday 09:14** — Em's markup opens with the note already bound in the preface, then the mechanical habit at scale, and the book comes back sounding like Hal.
4. **11:52** — "thesis" rejected, "footing" kept, applied to both passages, resolving nothing and locating everything.

I flagged beat three to Gus as the risk: it's where Em could tip into cruelty and where a reader stops believing her, and he's the one who'd feel it first. Four new facts entered the record there for Priya: the two passage contents, page 211, and the chapter numbers three and eleven.
